questions.question: Which type of ROM can be programmed only once after manufacturing?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**PROM**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **PROM** stands for **Programmable Read-Only Memory**.
 
• This type of **ROM** can be programmed **only once** after manufacturing.
 
• Once the data is written into a **PROM**, it becomes permanent and cannot be modified or erased.
 
• The programming of a **PROM** is done using a special device called a **PROM programmer**.
 
• **PROMs** are widely used in applications where the data needs to be permanently stored and protected from accidental changes.
 
• Unlike **EEPROM** or **EPROM**, a **PROM** does not allow reprogramming or erasing.
 
• It is typically used for storing **firmware** or **software instructions** in embedded systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **EEPROM**__

 __
 
• **EEPROM** stands for **Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory**.
 
• It allows data to be erased and rewritten multiple times using electrical signals.
 
• EEPROM is widely used in **devices requiring frequent updates**, such as microcontrollers and BIOS chips.
 
• It is slower compared to **flash memory** but provides more precise control over data erasure and writing.
 
 
 
• **Mask ROM**__
 __
 
• **Mask ROM** is a type of ROM where data is permanently written during the manufacturing process.
 
• It is not programmable by the user and is used for **fixed data storage**, such as in **video game cartridges**.
 
• Mask ROM is highly reliable but lacks flexibility since the data cannot be altered after production.
 
 
 
• **EPROM**__
 
 
• **EPROM** stands for **Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory**.
 
• Data written in an **EPROM** can be erased by exposing the chip to **ultraviolet light**.
 
• It is reusable, making it suitable for applications requiring periodic updates.
 
• EPROM chips have a transparent window through which the **UV light** is directed for erasing the data.

questions.question: Who first proposed a law in 1931 to clarify the idea of thermal equilibrium and its significance in determining temperature?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ralph H. Fowler**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ralph H. Fowler**, a British physicist, first proposed the law of thermal equilibrium in **1931**, which is known as the **Zeroeth Law of Thermodynamics**.
 
• The Zeroeth Law of Thermodynamics states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
 
• This law established the concept of **temperature** as a fundamental and measurable quantity.
 
• It plays a critical role in defining the basis for temperature measurement and classification of thermodynamic systems.
 
• The Zeroeth Law is essential for the proper functioning of **thermometers**, as it ensures that temperature readings are consistent across different systems.
 
• Ralph H. Fowler made significant contributions to statistical mechanics, thermodynamics, and astrophysics during his career.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Hugh L. Callendar**__

 __
 
• **Hugh Longbourne Callendar** was a British physicist known for his work on the properties of steam and on thermometry.
 
• He developed the **Callendar Steam Tables**, which provided detailed data on the thermodynamic properties of water and steam.
 
• He also invented the **Callendar Electrical Resistance Thermometer** for highly accurate temperature measurements.
 
 
 
• **James P. Espy**__
 __
 
• **James Pollard Espy** was an American meteorologist known as the "Storm King" for his studies on the formation and behavior of storms.
 
• He made significant contributions to the understanding of atmospheric thermodynamics and weather prediction.
 
• Espy's work focused on the processes of **condensation and latent heat release** in storm systems.
 
 
 
• **Rudolf Clausius**__
 
 
• **Rudolf Clausius** was a German physicist and mathematician, one of the founders of modern thermodynamics.
 
• He introduced the concept of **entropy** and formulated the **Second Law of Thermodynamics**.
 
• Clausius's work laid the foundation for the study of energy transformation and the directionality of processes.

questions.question: An infrasound microphone enables the remote detection of aircraft wake vortices, clear air turbulence, tornadoes, and seismic events at frequencies below:

__
 
• Infrasound refers to **sound waves** that have frequencies below the **audible range of human hearing**, typically less than **20 Hz**.
 
• An **infrasound microphone** is specifically designed to detect these low-frequency sound waves, which are often associated with **natural and man-made phenomena**.
 
• These microphones are used in monitoring and detecting events such as **aircraft wake vortices**, **clear air turbulence**, **tornadoes**, and **seismic activities**.
 
• Infrasound detection is crucial for applications like **aviation safety**, **weather forecasting**, and **earthquake monitoring**.
 
• Frequencies below **20 Hz** are ideal for detecting infrasound because they can **travel long distances** and bypass obstacles like mountains and buildings.
 
• Such low-frequency waves are also used in **scientific research** to study phenomena like **volcanic eruptions** and **meteor impacts**.

__

 __
 
• **30 Hz** is above the infrasound range and falls within the **audible range** of human hearing.
 
• This frequency range is not suitable for detecting phenomena like **tornadoes** or **seismic activities**, as these events produce much lower frequencies.
 
 
 
• **10 Hz**__
 __
 
• **10 Hz** is within the infrasound range but does not cover the full spectrum of infrasound detection used for various applications like **aircraft wake vortices**.
 
 
 
• **5 Hz**__

questions.question: Which of the following is considered a major social development outcome of India’s economic reforms since 1991?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Improvement in life expectancy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• India’s **economic reforms of 1991** marked a significant shift towards liberalization, privatization, and globalization.
 
• These reforms contributed to the **enhancement of social development indicators**, including an improvement in **life expectancy.**
 
• **Life expectancy** is the average number of years a person is expected to live based on prevailing mortality rates.
 
• Due to economic reforms, there was a significant increase in **healthcare investments, infrastructure, and access to medical facilities**, leading to better healthcare services.
 
• Improved access to resources, healthcare, sanitation, and education directly impacted the quality of life and longevity of individuals.
 
• India’s life expectancy increased from **around 57 years in 1991** to **approximately 70 years by 2023** (as per global statistics).
 
• Economic growth also contributed to **poverty reduction**, improving nutrition and access to essential services, which positively impacted life expectancy.
 
• Several government initiatives, such as the **National Health Mission**, focus on improving healthcare facilities in rural and urban areas, further boosting life expectancy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Increase in poverty rate**__

 __
 
• Post the economic reforms, the poverty rate in India has shown a declining trend rather than an increase.
 
• The reforms led to improved economic opportunities, job creation, and higher incomes for many sections of society.
 
• Programs like the **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA)** and targeted subsidies have contributed to poverty alleviation.
 
 
 
• **Widening of fiscal deficit**__
 __
 
• The fiscal deficit refers to the difference between the government’s total expenditure and its total revenue (excluding borrowings).
 
• While economic reforms initially led to an increase in fiscal deficit due to liberalization measures, subsequent reforms focused on fiscal consolidation and reducing deficits.
 
• Efforts like the **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act** were introduced to manage fiscal deficit effectively.
 
 
 
• **Decrease in literacy rate**__
 
 
• Contrary to the option, India’s literacy rate has significantly improved post-1991 economic reforms.
 
• Government schemes like **Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan** and **Right to Education (RTE)** aimed at universalizing education contributed to an increase in literacy rates.
 
• The literacy rate in India rose from **around 52% in 1991** to **approximately 77% by 2023** (as per various reports).

questions.question: Who was the last Viceroy of India who oversaw the partition of India before leaving?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Lord Mountbatten**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lord Mountbatten** was the last **Viceroy of India**, serving from February 1947 to August 1947.
 
• He was appointed to oversee the **transition of India from British rule to independence**.
 
• During his tenure, he played a significant role in the **partition of India** into two nations: **India and Pakistan**.
 
• The partition was accompanied by large-scale communal violence and displacement of millions of people.
 
• Mountbatten's plan for independence was known as the **Mountbatten Plan**, which outlined the division of the country based on religious lines.
 
• India achieved independence on **15 August 1947**, marking the end of British rule in India.
 
• Lord Mountbatten became the first **Governor-General of independent India**, serving from August 1947 to June 1948.
 
• He was closely involved in discussions with Indian leaders such as **Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, and Muhammad Ali Jinnah** during the partition process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Pethick Lawrence**__

 __
 
• **Frederick Pethick-Lawrence** was a British politician and a member of the **Cabinet Mission** sent to India in 1946.
 
• The Cabinet Mission aimed to discuss the transfer of power and devise a plan for India's independence.
 
• Pethick Lawrence was the **Secretary of State for India** at that time.
 
• He was not the last Viceroy but played a role in earlier discussions regarding India's future.
 
 
 
• **Lord Cripps**__
 __
 
• **Sir Stafford Cripps** was a British politician who led the **Cripps Mission** to India in 1942 during World War II.
 
• The mission proposed a plan for Indian self-government, which was rejected by Indian leaders.
 
• He was not involved in the partition of India but in earlier attempts to negotiate independence.
 
 
 
• **Lord Wavell**__
 
 
• **Lord Wavell** was the Viceroy of India from **1943 to 1947**, prior to Lord Mountbatten.
 
• He organized the **Simla Conference** in 1945 to discuss India's political future but failed to reach a consensus.
 
• Wavell's tenure saw the **Bengal famine of 1943** and significant political turmoil.
 
• He was replaced by Lord Mountbatten in February 1947 as British leaders felt a change was needed to ensure a smooth transition to independence.

questions.question: Which of the following Acts provides legal status to Lok Adalats in India?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** provides the legal framework for establishing Lok Adalats in India.
 
• Lok Adalats are also known as **"People's Court"**, which aim to provide inexpensive and expeditious justice.
 
• This Act ensures the **speedy resolution of disputes** and promotes the concept of amicable settlement.
 
• Under the Act, the decisions made by Lok Adalats are treated as **final and binding** on the parties involved.
 
• The Act empowers the Lok Adalats to deal with cases related to **civil, matrimonial, land, and labour disputes**, among others.
 
• Lok Adalats function under the supervision of the **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** and various State Legal Services Authorities.
 
• The Act guarantees legal aid to weaker sections of society, ensuring **equal access to justice**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Indian Penal Code, 1860**__

 __
 
• The **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** is the main criminal code of India.
 
• It deals with crimes and penalties but does not address alternative dispute resolution mechanisms like Lok Adalats.
 
• It was enacted during British rule and is still in use with several amendments.
 
 
 
• **Civil Procedure Code, 1908**__
 __
 
• The **Civil Procedure Code (CPC)** governs the procedures for adjudication of civil cases in India.
 
• It does not specifically establish Lok Adalats, but it provides mechanisms for amicable resolution of disputes like mediation.
 
 
 
• **Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996**__
 
 
• This Act governs **arbitration and conciliation proceedings** in India.
 
• While it provides a framework for alternative dispute resolution, it is distinct from Lok Adalats and does not provide the legal status of Lok Adalats.
 
• It focuses primarily on commercial disputes and private arbitration.

• The **Kesavananda Bharati case** is considered one of the most significant constitutional cases in Indian history.
 
• It established the **Basic Structure Doctrine**, which holds that the Parliament cannot amend the Constitution in a way that destroys its fundamental features.
 
• The case was filed by **Kesavananda Bharati**, a religious leader from Kerala, challenging certain land reform laws enacted by the state.
 
• The Supreme Court ruled that while Parliament has the power to amend the Constitution under **Article 368**, this power is limited by the doctrine of basic structure.
 
• The judgment emphasized features like the **sovereignty, democratic character, secularism, federalism, and independence of the judiciary** as integral to the basic structure.
 
• This landmark judgment acted as a safeguard against misuse of constitutional amendment powers and preserved the essence of the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• This case dealt with the validity of the First Amendment to the Constitution.

• **IC Golaknath vs State of Punjab (1967)**__
 __
 
• In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights.
 
• The judgment was later overturned in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
 
• This case paved the way for the debate that led to the basic structure doctrine.
 
 
 
• **Minerva Mills vs Union of India (1980)**__
 
 
• This case reinforced the basic structure doctrine established in the Kesavananda Bharati case.
 
• The Supreme Court struck down amendments that violated the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy.
 
• It further emphasized the limitations on Parliament's amending powers.

questions.question: Which of the following abbreviations is correctly matched with its meaning?

options.text: ASCII – Automated System for Computer Input

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**CD - Compact Disc**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **Compact Disc (CD)** is an optical disc used to store digital data.
 
• CDs were originally developed for storing **music and audio recordings**. Later, they were adapted to store other forms of data, including **software and video files.**
 
• The technology behind CDs was first introduced by **Sony and Philips** in the year **1982**.
 
• A standard CD has a storage capacity of around **700 MB** or **80 minutes of audio.**
 
• Data is stored on CDs using a **laser beam**, which etches microscopic pits onto the disc's surface.
 
• CDs are read using a **laser diode** in CD players or drives that detects the pits and converts them into electrical signals.
 
• Common types of CDs include **CD-ROM** (read-only), **CD-R** (recordable), and **CD-RW** (rewritable).
 
• CDs were widely used for **data storage, music distribution, and software installation** before being largely replaced by DVDs and digital storage mediums like USBs and cloud storage.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **ASCII – Automated System for Computer Input**__

 __
 
• The term **ASCII** stands for **American Standard Code for Information Interchange**, not "Automated System for Computer Input."
 
• It is a character encoding standard used for representing text in computers and electronic devices.
 
• ASCII assigns a unique numeric value to each character, symbol, and control code, typically in the range of **0 to 127**.
 
• It is widely used in programming and data transmission for its simplicity and efficiency.
 
 
 
• **LAN – Large Area Network**__
 __
 
• The term **LAN** stands for **Local Area Network**, not "Large Area Network."
 
• A LAN is a network that connects computers and devices within a **limited geographical area**, such as a home, office, or school.
 
• LANs typically use technologies like **Ethernet** or **Wi-Fi** for connectivity.
 
• They are used for sharing resources like printers, files, and internet access within the local network.
 
 
 
• **LAN – Local Area Node**__
 
 
• The term **LAN** does not stand for "Local Area Node." It stands for **Local Area Network**, as mentioned earlier.
 
• It is designed to operate within a **restricted area** and is popular for its high speed and low cost of setup.
 
• LANs can consist of **nodes**, which are devices connected to the network such as computers, servers, and peripherals.

__
 
• The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They are guidelines for the government to ensure socio-economic justice and aim to establish a **welfare state**.
 
• These principles are non-justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by courts, but they provide a framework for crafting policies and laws.
 
• The DPSPs draw inspiration from the **Irish Constitution** and reflect the ideals of the **Preamble**, such as justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.
 
• Article 38 of the Indian Constitution explicitly directs the state to promote the welfare of people by securing and protecting a social order based on justice, economic equality, and political equity.
 
• Examples of welfare measures rooted in DPSPs include **free legal aid** (Article 39A), promotion of education and public health (Article 47), and protection of the environment (Article 48A).
 
• The DPSPs aim to reduce inequalities, ensure equitable distribution of wealth, and provide opportunities for all citizens.

__
 
• **A capitalist state**__

 __
 
• A capitalist state is characterized by **private ownership** of the means of production and minimal intervention by the government in economic activities.
 
• The focus is on a free market economy, where resources are allocated based on **supply and demand**.
 
• While capitalism promotes economic growth and innovation, it often leads to income inequality, which is contrary to the ideals of the DPSPs.
 
 
 
• **A police state**__
 __
 
• A police state refers to a government that exercises excessive control over its citizens, often through the use of **authoritarian measures** and surveillance.
 
• Such states prioritize law enforcement and order over individual freedoms and rights, which is inconsistent with the principles of democracy and the welfare state envisioned in the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **A democratic dictatorship**__
 
 
• The term "democratic dictatorship" is contradictory, as democracy emphasizes **people's participation**, equality, and freedom, while dictatorship signifies **authoritarianism** and concentration of power.
 
• The Indian Constitution advocates a democratic system that ensures justice, equality, and liberty, which is incompatible with dictatorship.

questions.question: What is the term of office for the President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**5 years**__.

__
 
• The **President of India** is the **head of state** and the **supreme commander of the armed forces.**
 
• The term of office for the President of India is fixed at **5 years**, as per **Article 56 of the Indian Constitution.**
 
• After the completion of the term, the President is eligible for **re-election.**
 
• The election for the President is conducted by an **Electoral College**, which consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the Legislative Assemblies of States and Union territories.
 
• The President can, however, continue to hold office beyond the term of 5 years until their successor is elected and assumes office.
 
• The President may also resign before the expiration of their term by addressing their resignation to the **Vice-President of India.**
 
• The President can be removed from office before the expiry of their term through the process of **impeachment**, as mentioned in **Article 61 of the Indian Constitution.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Until removed by Parliament**__

 
 
• This option refers to the process of **removal or impeachment** of the President, which is a specific and formal process mentioned under **Article 61** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The President cannot remain in office indefinitely unless removed by Parliament. Their term is fixed at **5 years**, but removal is a separate process applicable only under specific circumstances like a violation of the Constitution.

questions.question: Which weathering process involves the peeling of rock layers due to temperature variations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Exfoliation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Exfoliation** is a weathering process where **rock layers peel off** or flake away due to repeated temperature variations.
 
• This process is also referred to as **onion-skin weathering** because of the way the rock surface peels off in layers.
 
• It typically occurs in areas with significant **diurnal temperature changes**, such as deserts.
 
• During the day, the rock surface heats up and expands, while at night it cools down and contracts, leading to stress on the rock.
 
• Over time, this repetitive expansion and contraction weaken the bonds in the outer layers of rock, causing them to flake off.
 
• The process is most prominent in rocks made of **granite** or other types of crystalline rocks.
 
• Exfoliation is a form of **mechanical weathering**, which involves the physical breakdown of rocks without any chemical alteration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Frost action**__

 __
 
• **Frost action**, also known as **freeze-thaw weathering**, occurs when water enters cracks in rocks, freezes, and expands.
 
• This expansion exerts pressure on the rock, causing it to break apart over time.
 
• It is common in cold climates where temperatures frequently fluctuate around the freezing point.
 
 
 
• **Solution**__
 __
 
• The **solution** process involves the chemical breakdown of rocks due to the dissolution of minerals in water.
 
• This process is particularly effective on rocks containing soluble minerals, such as **limestone**.
 
• It leads to the formation of features like **sinkholes** and **caves** in karst topography.
 
 
 
• **Oxidation**__
 
 
• **Oxidation** is a chemical weathering process that involves the reaction of minerals in rocks with **oxygen**.
 
• This process often leads to the formation of **rust**, especially in rocks containing iron.
 
• Oxidation is responsible for the reddish or orange coloration seen in many rocks and soils.
